01.note: Ulla, a Sage from the Land of Israel, came to Babylonia and saw flying clouds, which at home were a sure sign of rain. He told the local people to put away their vessels because rain was about to fall. No rain came. Ulla quipped that just as Babylonians are liars, so too their rains are liars.
01.why: The Gemara has just defined flying clouds, a thin cloud under a thick one, and Rabbi Yohanan called them a sign of coming rain; Ulla's visit shows the sign failing in Babylonia.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage visiting Babylonia, who reads the clouds as a sign of rain.

terms.meaning: A thin cloud beneath a thick cloud, described just before the story as a sign that rain is near.
The land of the Jewish community in Mesopotamia, where the Babylonian Talmud was composed; here contrasted with the Land of Israel.

02.note: On another visit to Babylonia, Ulla saw a whole basket of dates sold for a single coin. He remarked that with honey-sweet food so cheap, it was strange that the Babylonians did not occupy themselves with Torah. That night the dates gave him pain. He then said: a basket of knives for a coin, and still the Babylonians manage to study Torah.
02.why: This is the second of two short tales about Ulla in Babylonia, placed beside his complaint about Babylonian rain in a discussion of rain and its signs.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage in Babylonia who first mocks, then admires, the Babylonians' Torah study.

terms.meaning: A coin; here a small price for a large basket of dates.
Here, the study of Jewish teaching and law, the main occupation of the Sages.

03.note: Mar Ukva came to the city of Ginzak, and the people there asked him three questions: may one fast for just part of a day, are wine jars belonging to gentiles forbidden for good, and what did Moses wear when he served as priest during the seven days of inauguration. He had no answer ready for any of them. He went and asked in the study hall. They told him one may fast for hours and even say the fast-day prayer; gentiles' jars are permitted after twelve months; and Moses served in a white cloak. Rav Kahana taught that the cloak had no hem.
03.why: Rav Yosef and Abaye have just been debating whether Rav Huna holds that one may fast for only a few hours; the study hall's ruling to Mar Ukva gives the answer as the accepted law.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who visits Ginzak and cannot answer the townspeople's three questions until he asks in the study hall.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who adds that Moses' white cloak had no hem.

people.name: Moses
people.about: The subject of the third question: what he wore while serving as priest during the inauguration.

terms.meaning: Fasting for only part of a day rather than from morning to nightfall.
The week in which the Tabernacle was dedicated and Aaron and his sons were installed as priests, with Moses serving as priest.
Jewish law; the ruling that is followed in practice.
The house of study where the Sages gathered to learn and decide questions of law.

04.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, recalls that his family descends from Senaah of the tribe of Benjamin. One year the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat, so the fast was put off to the next day. His family fasted that day but did not finish the fast, because that day was a private family holiday of theirs.
04.why: Rav Hisda has ruled that a fast which does not last until sunset is not called a fast; the Gemara cites this family's half-day fast as a challenge, then answers that they fasted only to cause themselves distress.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who tells of his own family's practice; he says he is a descendant of Senaah of the tribe of Benjamin.

terms.meaning: The fast day mourning the destruction of the Temple. When it falls on Shabbat it is postponed, since one does not fast on Shabbat.
The Jewish Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which fasting is generally not allowed.

05.note: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi, visited the house of Rav Asi, where they prepared a choice calf for him and urged him to eat. He told them he was fasting. They asked why he did not borrow the fast and repay it on another day, as Rav taught. He answered that this was a fast for a dream.
05.why: Rav has just taught that a person may borrow his fast and repay it later. This visit tests that rule, and the Gemara then explains why a dream fast is an exception: it works only on the day of the dream.

people.name: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: A guest at Rav Asi's house who refuses a fine meal because he is fasting.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The host at whose house the meal is prepared.

terms.meaning: A calf considered especially choice meat, prepared for an honored guest.
Breaking a fast one took on for a given day and making it up by fasting on another day instead.
A fast kept to undo the effects of a bad dream.

06.note: Rabbi Abba the priest reported, in the name of Rabbi Yosei the priest, that the sons of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina, died, and he bathed in cold water through all seven days of mourning.
06.why: The Gemara is asking whether a mourner may bathe in cold water. It brings this case as proof, then answers that his sons died one after another, a situation in which mourners are allowed extra leniencies.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose sons died; he bathed in cold water during the mourning week.

people.name: Rabbi Abba the priest
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the priest
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is reported.

terms.meaning: The first week after a close relative's death, when mourners refrain from bathing, haircuts and other comforts.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

07.note: In the years of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, the community was struck by a trouble. He decreed thirteen fasts, but they were not answered, and he thought of decreeing more. Rabbi Ami told him that the Sages had said one must not trouble the community too much.
07.why: The mishna sets thirteen fasts as the limit; the Gemara uses this case to ask whether the limit applies to every calamity, and reports that Rabbi Ami acted on his own, against Rabbi Yohanan's view that the limit is only for rain.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The community leader who decreed thirteen fasts during a time of trouble.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage who warns him not to decree more fasts.

terms.meaning: From Nasi, the title of the head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
The full series of public fasts the mishna lays down when rain does not come.

08.note: The wicked Roman empire once forbade the Jews to study Torah, to circumcise their sons, and to keep Shabbat. Yehuda ben Shammua and his colleagues went to a Roman matron whom all the great men of Rome visited, and she told them to cry out at night. They did, calling out: O Heaven, are we not brothers, children of one father and one mother? Why are we different from every other nation, that you issue evil decrees against us? The decrees were annulled, and the day, the twenty-eighth of Adar, was made a holiday.
08.why: The Gemara is working out which days near the dates in Megillat Taanit are closed to fasting. It cites this story to show that the twenty-eighth of Adar is itself one of those dates.

people.name: Yehuda ben Shammua
people.about: A leader who, with his colleagues, seeks advice on how to overturn the Roman decrees.

people.name: A Roman matron
people.about: A woman whom all the prominent people of Rome visited; she advises the Jews to cry out at night.

terms.meaning: An ancient list of days on which fasting or eulogies were forbidden because something good happened to the Jews on them.
A government order forcing Jews to abandon Jewish practice.
The Hebrew month in late winter, the month of Purim.

09.note: Nicanor was a Greek general who waved his hand over Judea and Jerusalem every day, saying: When will this city fall into my hands, so I can trample it? When the Hasmonean kingdom defeated the Greeks, they cut off his thumbs and big toes and hung them on the gates of Jerusalem, saying that vengeance should be taken on the mouth that spoke with pride and the hands that waved over Jerusalem.
09.why: Rav Ashi has just asked whether a fast on the twelfth of Adar should be forbidden because it is the day before Nicanor's Day; the Gemara then explains where Nicanor's Day comes from.

people.name: Nicanor
people.about: A Greek general who threatened Jerusalem every day.

terms.meaning: The Jewish dynasty that rose up against Greek rule, the family behind the Hanukkah story.
A day of celebration marking his defeat, one of the dates on which fasting was forbidden.

10.note: Trajan was about to kill two leaders, Luleyanus and his brother Pappas, in Laodicea. He taunted them: if you are of the people of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, let your God save you from me as He saved them from Nebuchadnezzar. They answered that those three were wholly righteous and Nebuchadnezzar was a worthy king, while Trajan was a commoner and they themselves deserved death from God, who has many executioners, bears and lions. God had given them into his hands only to avenge their blood on him later. Trajan killed them at once. Before anyone had left the spot, two officials arrived from Rome and split his skull with clubs.
10.why: The Gemara is explaining the origin of Trajan's Day, raised because the twelfth of Adar fell on that day. It has said the day was later annulled, when Shemaya and his brother Ahiya were killed on it.

people.name: Trajan
people.about: The ruler who sets out to kill the two brothers and is himself killed.

people.name: Luleyanus
people.about: A leader Trajan seeks to kill; he and his brother answer Trajan's taunt.

people.name: Pappas
people.about: Brother of Luleyanus, killed with him.

people.name: Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah
people.about: Three righteous men God saved from Nebuchadnezzar, whom Trajan mentions to mock the brothers.

people.name: Nebuchadnezzar
people.about: A king the brothers call legitimate and so a fitting agent for a miracle, unlike Trajan.

terms.meaning: A day of celebration marking Trajan's death, once a day on which fasting was forbidden.
A name for God.

11.note: Once the pilgrims came to Jerusalem for a festival and there was no water to drink. Nakdimon ben Guryon borrowed twelve wells of water from a gentile officer, promising to return twelve wells of water by a set date or pay twelve talents of silver. The day came with no rain, and the officer sent for his payment morning, noon and afternoon, then went off happy to the bathhouse. Nakdimon went sadly to the Temple and prayed that he had acted for God's honor, and rain fell until the cisterns overflowed. The officer claimed the sun had set, so the money was still his. Nakdimon prayed again, the clouds scattered and the sun shone. A Sage taught that his real name was Buni, and he was called Nakdimon because the sun broke through for him.
11.why: The Gemara has been comparing years of plentiful and scarce rain. Right after the story it lists three people for whom the sun broke through out of time: Moses, Joshua and Nakdimon.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: A wealthy man of Jerusalem who borrows water for the pilgrims and prays for rain to repay it.

people.name: The officer
people.about: A gentile official who lends the water and demands payment.

terms.meaning: One of the three festivals (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot) when Jews traveled to Jerusalem to the Temple.
A very large weight of silver, a huge sum of money.
A Greek word for a ruler or officer, used here for the gentile official.

12.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, was riding his donkey along a riverbank, coming from his teacher's house, full of pride at how much Torah he had learned. A very ugly man greeted him, and instead of answering he said: Worthless one, are all the people of your city as ugly as you? The man told him to go tell the Craftsman who made him how ugly His vessel was. Rabbi Elazar got down, bowed before him and begged forgiveness, but the man refused, and the rabbi followed him to the rabbi's own city. When the townspeople greeted the rabbi, the man said: may there not be many like him in Israel. At their request he forgave him, on condition he not make a habit of it. Rabbi Elazar then went in and taught that a person should be soft as a reed, not stiff as a cedar.
12.why: The Gemara has just praised the reed above the cedar, explaining why Ahijah's comparison of Israel to a reed is better than Balaam's comparison to a cedar; this story gives the same teaching through the reed's softness.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage returning from his teacher, proud of his learning, who insults a stranger.

people.name: The ugly man
people.about: A stranger insulted by the rabbi, who sends him to complain to the Craftsman who made him.

terms.meaning: The man's way of speaking of God as his maker.
A pen cut from a reed, used to write Torah scrolls.
Phylacteries (tefillin) are small boxes of scripture worn in prayer; mezuzot are scrolls fixed to doorposts. Both are handwritten.

13.note: Rav Huna had wine stored in a crumbling house and wanted to move it out. He brought Rav Adda bar Ahava inside and kept him there in a long discussion of law until all the wine was out. As soon as they left, the house fell down. Rav Adda bar Ahava understood what had happened and was angry.
13.why: Just before, Rav felt safe passing a dangerous wall because Rav Adda bar Ahava's merit was great. Afterward the Gemara explains his anger: Rabbi Yannai warns that a miracle done for a person is deducted from his merits.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who uses Rav Adda bar Ahava's presence to protect his wine in a falling house.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage whose merit was thought to protect those near him; he is angry when he realizes he was used this way.

terms.meaning: The credit a person earns through good deeds, which was believed to protect him and those around him.

14.note: Ilfa and Rabbi Yohanan studied Torah together and grew very poor, so they set out to go into business. Sitting under a crumbling wall eating bread, Rabbi Yohanan heard two angels talking: one wanted to knock the wall down and kill them for leaving the eternal life of Torah, and the other said to leave them, since one of them had a great time ahead of him. Ilfa heard nothing, so Rabbi Yohanan concluded he was the one, and went back to study. By the time Ilfa returned, Rabbi Yohanan had become head of the academy. Told he would have led too if he had stayed, Ilfa hung from a ship's mast and declared he would fall and drown if anyone asked about the baraitot of Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya and he could not answer from a mishna. An old man came and put a case to him about a dying man's will.
14.why: The Gemara has been telling stories about Rav Huna's acts of kindness; this one begins a run of stories set beside a falling wall or a crumbling house.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Ilfa's study partner, who overhears the angels, goes back to study, and becomes head of the academy.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's study partner, who goes into business and later proves he has kept his learning.

people.name: A certain old man
people.about: The man who takes up Ilfa's challenge and puts a legal case to him.

terms.meaning: Angels who serve God; here two of them debate whether to kill the two scholars.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna; Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya were known for collecting them.
The first written collection of Jewish law, on which the Talmud is built.
Coins; a sela is worth twice a shekel.

14.flag: The story stops after the old man's question; Ilfa's answer, which ends the episode, is in the next segment and is cut off from the story.

15.note: Nahum of Gam Zu was blind, had lost both hands and both legs, and was covered in boils. He lay in a crumbling house with his bed legs in bowls of water to keep ants off. He told his students to carry out his things before his bed, since the house would not fall while he was in it; they did, and once his bed was out the house fell. They asked why so righteous a man suffered so. He said he had brought it on himself: on the road with three loaded donkeys, a poor man begged him for food, and he said to wait while he unloaded. The man died before he finished. Nahum fell on him and prayed that his own eyes, hands and legs be lost and his body covered in boils. When his students cried woe that they saw him so, he said: woe to me if you had not.
15.why: The Gemara is telling a run of stories about crumbling walls and houses, after the dilapidated wall in the story of Ilfa and Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Nahum of Gam Zu
people.about: A righteous teacher, blind and maimed, whose presence keeps a falling house standing.

people.name: His students
people.about: Students who carry him from the house and ask why he suffers.

people.name: A poor person
people.about: A man who begged Nahum for food on the road and died before he was fed.

terms.meaning: Painful skin sores, here covering his whole body.

16.note: Nahum of Gam Zu got his name because whatever happened, he said: this too is for the good. The Jews sent him to the emperor with a chest of jewels as a gift. At an inn on the way, people stole the jewels and filled the chest with earth. The emperor wanted to kill them all for mocking him, and Nahum said: this too is for the good. Elijah appeared as one of the ministers and suggested the earth was Abraham's, which turned into swords when thrown. Tested on a province they had failed to conquer, it won the battle, so the emperor filled the chest with jewels and sent Nahum off with honor. The innkeepers then tore down their inn and brought its soil to the king, but it worked no wonders, and the king had them killed.
16.why: The Gemara has just told of Nahum's suffering and the house that did not fall while he was in it, and now explains how he got his name.

people.name: Nahum of Gam Zu
people.about: A Sage sent to the emperor with a gift, who says this too is for the good whatever happens.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as one of the emperor's ministers and saves the Jews.

people.name: The emperor
people.about: The ruler who receives the chest of earth and first wants to kill the Jews.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: The forefather, whose earth Elijah claims turned into swords when thrown.

terms.meaning: Hebrew for this too is for the good, Nahum's saying and the source of his name.
A Greek word for a gift, here a gift to the emperor.

17.note: A plague broke out in Sura, but Rav's neighborhood was spared. People thought it was because of Rav's great merit. A dream revealed to them that this was too small a matter for Rav's merit. Rather, the neighborhood was spared because of a certain man who lent out his hoe and shovel for digging graves.
17.why: The mishna has just defined when deaths in a city count as a plague requiring a fast; the Gemara follows with stories about plagues and the merits of ordinary people.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A great Sage whose neighborhood in Sura escaped the plague; people credited it to his merit.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: An ordinary man who lent his hoe and shovel for burials, whose merit truly saved the neighborhood.

terms.meaning: The credit a person earns through good deeds, which was believed to protect him and those around him.
A Jewish town in Babylonia.

18.note: A fire broke out in Drokart, but Rav Huna's neighborhood was spared. People thought it was because of Rav Huna's great merit. A dream revealed to them that this was too small a matter for Rav Huna. Rather, it was because of a certain woman who heated her oven and let her neighbors use it.
18.why: It follows a matching story about the plague in Sura, in which an ordinary man's kindness, not Rav's merit, protected the neighborhood.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage whose neighborhood was spared from the fire; people credited it to his merit.

people.name: A certain woman
people.about: A neighbor who lent the use of her heated oven, whose merit truly spared the neighborhood.

terms.meaning: The credit a person earns through good deeds, which was believed to protect him and those around him.

19.note: People told Rav Yehuda that locusts had come, and he decreed a fast. They told him the locusts were not destroying anything. He answered: did they bring provisions with them?
19.why: The Gemara is listing cases in which Sages decreed a fast for a calamity that seemed minor or distant, illustrating the mishna's rules on fasting for plagues.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who decrees a fast when locusts arrive, though they are not yet doing damage.

terms.meaning: Ordered the community to fast and pray, a response to a threatened disaster.

20.note: Abba the Bloodletter received greetings from the heavenly academy every day, Abaye every Shabbat eve, and Rava only on the eve of Yom Kippur. Abaye was upset and was told he could not do what Abba did. Abba treated men and women separately, gave women a slit garment so he would not see them, and kept a hidden box for fees so the poor were not shamed. He charged Torah scholars nothing and gave them money for food. Abaye sent two Sages to test him. Abba fed them and spread rugs for them, and in the morning they took the rugs to the market. Asked the price, he named what he had paid. Told the rugs were his, he explained he had assumed they needed money to ransom captives and were ashamed to ask, and had already given the rugs to charity in his mind.
20.why: The Gemara has been telling how the merit of ordinary people, like the man who lent tools for burials, can surpass that of great Sages; this story makes the same point.

people.name: Abba the Bloodletter
people.about: A bloodletter, a kind of healer, greeted from Heaven daily for his modesty and generosity.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage greeted from Heaven each Shabbat eve, upset that Abba is honored more; he sends two Sages to test him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage greeted from Heaven only once a year.

terms.meaning: A healer who drew blood from patients, a common medical treatment in ancient times.
The heavenly academy, imagined as a gathering of Sages in Heaven.
Paying to free Jews held captive, considered among the greatest acts of charity.
